All of this token's backing, 100.0% of it, sits in the checkable on-chain class, meaning anyone can verify the collateral's value directly on the chain without trusting a wrapper or a company's paperwork. The collateral behind that entire share is ETH, held at the terminal layer. There is nothing in the one-layer-down wrapped class and nothing in the disclosure-dependent class, so there is no reliance on published statements from an issuer or custodian, and no staleness question arises there — the staleness status confirms there are no disclosure-dependent nodes to go stale.

Because the backing is entirely ETH tracked on-chain, there is no depth-truncated share to worry about and no unclassified portion pending review; both sit at 0. The perimeter covers all troves with an exact identity, and the traced collateral value stands at $183.5M against a backed supply of $26.2M, so the checkable collateral more than covers the supply it backs.

The admin qualifier banner states that no admin power can alter backing, describing it as immutable. In other words, there is no governance process, delay, or authorized party that can change what backs this token — the backing composition itself is fixed by design rather than by a rule that officials could vote to amend.

For LUSD, the mechanism that matters in a collateral crash is the Stability Pool. When a trove's collateral ratio falls below the minimum, the Pool absorbs its debt directly, paying out collateral to Pool depositors; any shortfall the Pool cannot cover is redistributed pro rata onto surviving troves rather than sold into the market. Redemptions against troves are a separate channel, but on this scenario that path is excluded, so no redemption capacity is counted.

Bad debt is $0, and the collateral that must be sold is $0 against exit liquidity of $8.8M, giving a forced-sales-to-exit-liquidity ratio of 0.

Bad debt is structurally zero on this grid: no trove reaches the minimum collateral ratio under the shocks modelled here. The first liquidation would only occur at an ETH shock of -81.63% (minimum ICR falling from 5.9890 to 1.1), Recovery Mode would only engage at -78.56% (system collateral ratio falling from 6.9968 to 1.5), and the system collateral ratio would only fall below the minimum collateral ratio at -84.28%. Liquity v1 itself is wound down to 72 troves, which is part of why no positions are engaged on this grid.

Since no forced sale occurs, the redistributed debt figure and the redistributed-positions-below-100 figure, which is how bad debt is defined for LUSD, are both $0, and the exit liquidity of $8.8M is untouched rather than exhausted in this scenario.

This test asks what happens if the paired stablecoin used in exit venues, referenced here as the Member-2 target, slips away from its own dollar peg. Because this token is structurally insulated, that kind of depeg cannot force a mechanical sale of the token itself: the assumptions describe it as structurally insulated, exposed through exit venues only. So there is no minting or redemption path that dumps supply just because the paired stablecoin wobbles.

That does not mean the token is unaffected. What changes instead is how much you could actually sell without moving the price much, because that liquidity sits in pools priced against the paired stablecoin. In the headline scenario, with the paired stablecoin at its middle target and no liquidity-provider flight, forced sales in the Member-2 headline depeg scenario come out at $0, exit liquidity in that same scenario is $8.2M, and the resulting ratio is 0. The zero forced-sales figure reflects the mechanism's design, not an absence of exposure.

The exit-liquidity curves show how the venue itself degrades as the paired stablecoin's price target worsens. At the mild target of 0.93, exit liquidity ranges from $6.9M at a 0.5% price impact up to $8.7M at 5.0%. At the deeper target of 0.88, the same curve runs from $6.5M to $8.2M, and at the milder target of 0.97 it runs from $7.2M up to $9.0M. As the paired stablecoin's target price falls, the depth available at any given price impact shrinks, meaning holders would face thinner exit liquidity and larger price impact for the same size of sale, even though no forced selling of the token itself is triggered by construction.
